claim: Almost all individuals with diabetes will develop some form of diabetic retinopathy over time.
source: Almost all individuals with diabetes will develop some form of diabetic retinopathy over time (National Diabetes Fact Sheet, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to National Diabetes Fact Sheet, 2011

claim: In the United States diabetic retinopathy is the most frequent cause of blindness among working age individuals.
source: In the United States diabetic retinopathy is the most frequent cause of blindness among working age individuals (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2018

claim: Phenotypic variation in diabetic retinopathy is influenced by two primary risk factors: the duration of diabetes and an individual's level of glycemia (HbA1c).
source: Epidemiological studies suggest that phenotypic variation is influenced by two primary risk factors: the duration of diabetes and an individual's level of glycemia (HbA1c) (DCCT/EDIC Research Group et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to DCCT/EDIC Research Group et al., 2017

claim: Duration of diabetes and level of glycemic control do not completely explain an individual's risk for developing diabetic retinopathy.
source: However, these two factors do not completely explain an individual's risk for developing diabetic retinopathy.
evidence: Supported by clinical observations and epidemiological context

claim: Some individuals with diabetes develop very minimal retinopathy.
source: Moreover, some individuals with diabetes develop very minimal retinopathy (Sun et al., 2011), whereas others clearly seem to have a predisposition for severe retinopathy (Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2011

claim: Some individuals with diabetes have a predisposition for severe retinopathy.
source: Moreover, some individuals with diabetes develop very minimal retinopathy (Sun et al., 2011), whereas others clearly seem to have a predisposition for severe retinopathy (Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao et al., 2014

claim: Genetic factors account for 25–50% of an individual's risk of developing severe diabetic retinopathy.
source: Familial aggregation and twin studies estimate that genetic factors account for 25–50% of an individual's risk of developing severe diabetic retinopathy (Arar et al., 2008; Hietala et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arar et al., 2008 and Hietala et al., 2008

claim: Diabetic retinopathy is a highly polygenic trait influenced by multiple genetic variants of small effect.
source: Genetic studies suggest that it is a highly polygenic trait influenced by multiple genetic variants of small effect.
evidence: Supported by genetic studies and established knowledge

claim: A majority of genetic variants nominally associated with diabetic retinopathy are located in intronic or inter-genic regions.
source: Notably, like other complex disease traits including age-related macular degeneration (Fritsche et al., 2014; Fritsche et al., 2016), a majority of genetic variants nominally associated with diabetic retinopathy are located in intronic or inter-genic regions (Risch and Merikangas, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fritsche et al., 2014; Fritsche et al., 2016; and Risch and Merikangas, 1996

claim: Most genetic variants associated with diabetic retinopathy play critically important functional roles in regulating gene expression.
source: Most of these variants appear to play critically important functional roles in regulating gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from the location of variants and their functional context

claim: Several of the top associated SNPs identified in the meta-GWAS of diabetic retinopathy are present in DNase hypersensitivity sites and affect gene expression levels by altering the allelic chromatin state or the binding sites of transcription factors.
source: In fact, several of the top associated SNPs identified in our meta-GWAS of diabetic retinopathy (Grassi et al., 2011) are present in DNase hypersensitivity sites and affect gene expression levels by altering the allelic chromatin state or the binding sites of transcription factors (Maurano et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grassi et al., 2011 and Maurano et al., 2012

claim: Disease-associated genetic loci often influence gene expression levels.
source: The observation that disease-associated genetic loci often influence gene expression levels (Gamazon et al., 2018) led us to postulate that integrating gene expression with genetic association would be a powerful approach to identify susceptibility genes for diabetic retinopathy.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamazon et al., 2018

claim: Individuals with retinopathy (PDR) show differences in diabetes duration compared to individuals without retinopathy (nDR).
source: As anticipated, notable differences were observed between individuals with and without retinopathy (PDR vs. nDR) for mean duration of diabetes (53 ± 43.4 months vs. 27 ± 13.4 months).
evidence: Supported by data from matched DCCT/EDIC participants

claim: Individuals with retinopathy (PDR) show differences in level of glycemia (HbA1c) compared to individuals without retinopathy (nDR).
source: mean HbA1c (9.71 ± 2.37 vs. 7.62 ± 1.07) given their significant impact on retinopathy.
evidence: Supported by data from matched DCCT/EDIC participants

claim: 22% of 11,548 examined genes demonstrated a differential response in expression between standard glucose and high glucose conditions.
source: We observed that 22% of 11,548 examined genes demonstrated a differential response in expression between the two conditions (true positive rate; π1 = 0.22) (Storey and Tibshirani, 2003; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with 299 of those at an FDR < 0.05 (Figure 1a), supporting a significant impact of glucose on the LCL transcriptome.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: 299 genes showed differential response to glucose at an FDR < 0.05.
source: We observed that 22% of 11,548 examined genes demonstrated a differential response in expression between the two conditions (true positive rate; π1 = 0.22) (Storey and Tibshirani, 2003; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with 299 of those at an FDR < 0.05 (Figure 1a), supporting a significant impact of glucose on the LCL transcriptome.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1a

claim: Interindividual transcriptome response to high glucose is greater than the intraindividual response.
source: We confirmed that interindividual transcriptome response to HG is greater than the intraindividual response (p=2×10−16) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p-value and shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2, 3, and 4

claim: TXNIP exhibited the largest and most significant transcriptional response to glucose.
source: Interestingly, TXNIP, the most highly glucose-inducible gene in multiple cell types (Devi et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2016), exhibited the largest (log2(FC) difference = 0.2) and most significant (p=3.2×10−12, FDR = 5.1×10−8) transcriptional response to glucose.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data and citations to Devi et al., 2017 and Chen et al., 2016

claim: TXNIP is the most highly glucose-inducible gene in multiple cell types.
source: Interestingly, TXNIP, the most highly glucose-inducible gene in multiple cell types (Devi et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2016), exhibited the largest (log2(FC) difference = 0.2) and most significant (p=3.2×10−12, FDR = 5.1×10−8) transcriptional response to glucose.
evidence: Supported by citations to Devi et al., 2017 and Chen et al., 2016

claim: Genes involved in DNA packaging are dramatically upregulated in response to glucose.
source: Pathway analysis using gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed dramatic upregulation of genes involved in structural changes to DNA (DNA packaging, FDR < 0.0001) and in genes such as transcription factors that modulate the cellular response to environmental stimuli (protein DNA complex, FDR < 0.0001) (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1b

claim: Genes such as transcription factors that modulate the cellular response to environmental stimuli are dramatically upregulated in response to glucose.
source: Pathway analysis using gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed dramatic upregulation of genes involved in structural changes to DNA (DNA packaging, FDR < 0.0001) and in genes such as transcription factors that modulate the cellular response to environmental stimuli (protein DNA complex, FDR < 0.0001) (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1b

claim: Genes that modulate the cellular response to infection are considerably downregulated in response to glucose.
source: Conversely, genes that modulate the cellular response to infection were considerably downregulated (type 1 interferon, FDR < 0.0001; gamma interferon, FDR < 0.0001; leukocyte chemotaxis genes, FDR < 0.0001) potentially supporting earlier work that chronic glucose exposure depresses cellular immune responsiveness (Delamaire et al., 1997; Al-Mashat et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis and citations to Delamaire et al., 1997 and Al-Mashat et al., 2006

claim: Chronic glucose exposure depresses cellular immune responsiveness.
source: Conversely, genes that modulate the cellular response to infection were considerably downregulated (type 1 interferon, FDR < 0.0001; gamma interferon, FDR < 0.0001; leukocyte chemotaxis genes, FDR < 0.0001) potentially supporting earlier work that chronic glucose exposure depresses cellular immune responsiveness (Delamaire et al., 1997; Al-Mashat et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delamaire et al., 1997 and Al-Mashat et al., 2006

claim: The observed interindividual variance in transcriptional response to glucose is dominated by randomized DCCT treatment group effects based on retinopathy status.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated that the observed interindividual variance is dominated by randomized DCCT treatment (intensive vs. conventional) group effects based on retinopathy status (p=3×10−6) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and is not confounded by LCL growth rate (p>0.05) or EBV-(Epstein Barr virus) copy number (p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis with p-value shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The observed interindividual variance in transcriptional response to glucose is not confounded by LCL growth rate.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated that the observed interindividual variance is dominated by randomized DCCT treatment (intensive vs. conventional) group effects based on retinopathy status (p=3×10−6) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and is not confounded by LCL growth rate (p>0.05) or EBV-(Epstein Barr virus) copy number (p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis with p-value

claim: The observed interindividual variance in transcriptional response to glucose is not confounded by EBV copy number.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated that the observed interindividual variance is dominated by randomized DCCT treatment (intensive vs. conventional) group effects based on retinopathy status (p=3×10−6) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and is not confounded by LCL growth rate (p>0.05) or EBV-(Epstein Barr virus) copy number (p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis with p-value

claim: 103 genes exhibit a differential glucose response between individuals with and without retinopathy at p<0.01.
source: Using a gene-wise analysis we identified 103 genes exhibiting a differential glucose response between individuals with and without retinopathy (p<0.01) (Figure 2; Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by gene-wise analysis shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1b

claim: IL1B is one of the top differential response genes between individuals with and without retinopathy.
source: One of the top differential response genes was IL1B (p=0.008, log2(FC) response difference = 0.289).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data with p-value and fold change

claim: Expression of IL1B is induced by high glucose.
source: Expression of IL1B has been previously reported to be induced by HG (Shanmugam et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shanmugam et al., 2003

claim: The expression of IL1B is upregulated in the diabetic retina and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy.
source: Additionally, the expression of IL1B is upregulated in the diabetic retina and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012

claim: PDGF signaling is the most significant differential response pathway between individuals with and without retinopathy.
source: We identified PDGF signaling as the most significant differential response pathway (FDR = 0.012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Elevated levels of PDGF are present in the vitreous of individuals with proliferative diabetic retinopathy compared to individuals without diabetes.
source: Elevated levels of PDGF are present in the vitreous of individuals with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) compared to individuals without diabetes (Freyberger et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Freyberger et al., 2000

claim: PDGF is required for normal blood vessel maintenance.
source: As PDGF is required for normal blood vessel maintenance, it is thought to contribute to the pericyte loss, microaneurysms, and acellular capillaries that are key features of the diabetic retina (Hammes et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hammes et al., 2002

claim: PDGF contributes to the pericyte loss, microaneurysms, and acellular capillaries that are key features of the diabetic retina.
source: As PDGF is required for normal blood vessel maintenance, it is thought to contribute to the pericyte loss, microaneurysms, and acellular capillaries that are key features of the diabetic retina (Hammes et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hammes et al., 2002

claim: Differential response genes are more likely to harbor eSNPs and be eGenes compared to the genome-wide average.
source: Differential response genes are more likely to harbor eSNPs, and hence be eGenes, compared to the genome-wide average (p=2.0×10−16) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p-value shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Differential response genes are more likely to be genetically regulated and may contribute to interindividual differences in the development of diabetic retinopathy.
source: This suggests that differential response genes are more likely to be genetically regulated and may contribute to interindividual differences in the development of diabetic retinopathy.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that differential response genes are more likely to be eGenes

claim: 7253 eSNPs from the differential response genes are enriched for association with diabetic retinopathy at FDR < 0.05.
source: The 7253 eSNPs from the differential response genes are enriched for association with diabetic retinopathy (FDR < 0.05) (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by GWAS analysis shown in Figure 3b

claim: Less than 1% of random sets of 103 genes contained the same proportion of similarly skewed GWAS p-values as the differential response genes.
source: To further assess the significance of this enrichment, we performed permutation testing of eSNPs from random sets of 103 genes which demonstrated that less than 1% contained the same proportion of similarly skewed GWAS p-values (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by permutation testing shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The eSNPs for differential response genes were enriched among diabetic retinopathy meta-GWAS p-values relative to all eSNPs.
source: The eSNPs for differential response genes were enriched among diabetic retinopathy meta-GWAS p-values relative to all eSNPs (p=0.0012) and all SNPs (p=0.0023) (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p-values shown in Figure 3c

claim: The eSNPs for differential response genes were enriched among diabetic retinopathy meta-GWAS p-values relative to all SNPs.
source: The eSNPs for differential response genes were enriched among diabetic retinopathy meta-GWAS p-values relative to all eSNPs (p=0.0012) and all SNPs (p=0.0023) (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p-values shown in Figure 3c

claim: Some of the genes exhibiting a differential response to glucose are associated with the development of severe diabetic retinopathy.
source: Thus, some of the genes exhibiting a differential response to glucose (RGpdr–ndr) are associated with the development of severe diabetic retinopathy.
evidence: Inferred from the enrichment of eSNPs for association with diabetic retinopathy

claim: rs11867934 is the most significant retinopathy-associated eSNP among the set of 7253 eSNPs tested.
source: The most significant retinopathy-associated eSNP among the set of 7253 eSNPs tested is rs11867934 (Figure 4a); FDR < 0.05; meta-GWAS p=6.7×10−6<Bonferroni adjusted p-value of 6.9 × 10−6; OR = 0.86, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.71,1.00; minor allele frequency = 0.22.
evidence: Supported by GWAS analysis shown in Figure 4a

claim: rs11867934 is an intergenic eSNP for FLCN in multiple biologically relevant tissues including artery and nerve.
source: rs11867934 is an intergenic eSNP for FLCN in multiple biologically relevant tissues including artery and nerve.
evidence: Supported by eQTL data from GTEx

claim: FLCN is expressed in the retina of human donor eyes.
source: We confirmed FLCN expression in the retina of human donor eyes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: FLCN was upregulated in response to glucose to a greater extent in individuals with diabetic retinopathy than in individuals with diabetes without retinopathy.
source: In the LCLs derived from individuals with diabetes, FLCN was upregulated in response to glucose to a greater extent in individuals with diabetic retinopathy than in individuals with diabetes without retinopathy (log2FC difference = 0.27, p=2.5×10−3) (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1b, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2, Supplementary file 1b, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: At least 43% of retina eQTLs are also eQTLs in GTEx LCLs.
source: We determined that at least 43% of retina eQTLs are also eQTLs in GTEx LCLs.
evidence: Supported by comparison of retina eQTLs and GTEx LCL eQTLs

claim: FLCN eSNPs (n = 272 eSNPs significant in the retina and 20 or more GTEx tissues) show an enrichment for association with diabetic retinopathy in the meta-GWAS.
source: We assessed the aggregated association of FLCN eSNPs (n = 272 eSNPs significant in the retina and 20 or more GTEx tissues) with diabetic retinopathy in the meta-GWAS and observed an enrichment for association with diabetic retinopathy (π1 = 0.9; Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by GWAS analysis shown in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: FLCN eSNPs were enriched for association with diabetic retinopathy in the UK Biobank.
source: We then validated the FLCN association with diabetic retinopathy in a third cohort, the UK Biobank (UKBB) (Supplementary file 1c), and found that the FLCN eSNPs were enriched for association with diabetic retinopathy in the UKBB (π1 = 0.73) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by GWAS analysis in UKBB shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: A one standard deviation increase in the predicted retinal expression of FLCN increases the risk of diabetic retinopathy by 0.15 SD.
source: A one standard deviation (SD) increase in the predicted retinal expression of FLCN increases the risk of diabetic retinopathy by 0.15 SD (95% CI: 0.02–0.29, standard error 0.07, p=0.024).
evidence: Supported by Mendelian randomization analysis

claim: Individuals with diabetes with high predicted retinal FLCN expression have increased odds of developing retinopathy.
source: Individuals with diabetes with high predicted retinal FLCN expression have increased odds of developing retinopathy (1.3 OR increase per SD increase in FLCN expression) (Chinn, 2000).
evidence: Supported by Mendelian randomization analysis and citation to Chinn, 2000

claim: There is no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy confounding the Mendelian randomization analysis of FLCN and diabetic retinopathy.
source: We did not observe any evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (in which FLCN eSNPs are independently associated with both FLCN expression and diabetic retinopathy) confounding the analysis [HEIDI p>0.05 (p=0.2)] (Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by HEIDI test with p-value and citation to Zhu et al., 2016

claim: There is an aggregated effect of 14 independent FLCN eQTLs on the development of diabetic retinopathy through FLCN expression.
source: We detected an aggregated effect of 14 independent FLCN eQTLs (r2 < 0.2) on the development of diabetic retinopathy through FLCN expression using multi-SNP Mendelian randomization (p=0.04) (Wu et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by multi-SNP Mendelian randomization analysis with p-value and citation to Wu et al., 2018a

claim: Genetic variation at the FLCN locus affects both FLCN expression and the development of diabetic retinopathy through the expression of FLCN.
source: Together, these findings support the presence of genetic variation at the FLCN locus affecting both FLCN expression and the development of diabetic retinopathy through the expression of FLCN.
evidence: Inferred from Mendelian randomization and genetic association results

claim: TXNIP is a key marker of oxidative stress.
source: For instance, TXNIP was identified as the top differential response gene to glucose in all individuals (RGall). TXNIP is a key marker of oxidative stress.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge

claim: TXNIP is upregulated in the diabetic retina where it induces Muller cell activation.
source: It is upregulated in the diabetic retina where it induces Muller cell activation (Devi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Devi et al., 2017

claim: High glucose treatment increases TXNIP expression.
source: HG treatment has been shown to increase TXNIP expression (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016

claim: TXNIP is a glucose sensor whose expression has been strongly associated with both hyperglycemia and diabetic complications.
source: TXNIP is a glucose sensor whose expression has been strongly associated with both hyperglycemia and diabetic complications.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge

claim: The TXNIP locus was differentially methylated in the primary leukocytes of EDIC cases and controls.
source: Specifically, the TXNIP locus was differentially methylated in the primary leukocytes of EDIC cases and controls (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016

claim: The cellular response to chronic glucose stress involves alterations in DNA accessibility which facilitates the gene expression response to this environmental stimulus.
source: The GSEA showed that the cellular response to chronic glucose stress involves alterations in DNA accessibility which facilitates the gene expression response to this environmental stimulus (Smith and Workman, 2012).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis and citation to Smith and Workman, 2012

claim: The transcriptional response to glucose in part manifests as diminished immune responsiveness, a well-characterized feature of diabetes.
source: The transcriptional response to glucose in part manifests as diminished immune responsiveness, a well-characterized feature of diabetes (Shanmugam et al., 2003; Mowat and Baum, 1971).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data and citations to Shanmugam et al., 2003 and Mowat and Baum, 1971

claim: FLCN is a biologically plausible diabetic retinopathy disease gene since its expression is present in both neuronal and vascular cells of the retina.
source: FLCN is a biologically plausible diabetic retinopathy disease gene since its expression is present in both neuronal and vascular cells of the retina.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing FLCN expression in retina

claim: FLCN is a negative regulator of AMPK which helps to modulate the energy sensing ability of AMPK and plays a role in responding to cellular stress.
source: Current evidence suggests that FLCN is a negative regulator of AMPK which helps to modulate the energy sensing ability of AMPK and plays a role in responding to cellular stress (Hasumi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hasumi et al., 2012

claim: AMPK plays an important role in providing resistance to cellular stresses by regulating autophagy and cellular bioenergetics to avoid apoptosis.
source: AMPK plays an important role in providing resistance to cellular stresses by regulating autophagy and cellular bioenergetics to avoid apoptosis.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge

claim: Loss of FLCN results in constitutive activation of AMPK.
source: Loss of FLCN results in constitutive activation of AMPK.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge

claim: Higher levels of FLCN would suggest less cellular capacity to deal with stress.
source: Higher levels of FLCN would suggest less cellular capacity to deal with stress (Possik et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Possik et al., 2014

claim: The protective effect of agents such as metformin and fenofibrate on diabetic retinopathy might be mediated through AMPK.
source: Interestingly, the protective effect of agents such as metformin and fenofibrate on diabetic retinopathy might be mediated through AMPK (Kim et al., 2007; Joe et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2007 and Joe et al., 2015

claim: White blood cells are readily accessible from the peripheral circulation of human patients and can reveal differential molecular characteristics depending on the stage of diabetic retinopathy.
source: First, we utilized white blood cells which are readily accessible from the peripheral circulation of human patients (Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) Research Group, 1999) and can reveal differential molecular characteristics depending on the stage of diabetic retinopathy (Tang and Kern, 2011; Gubitosi-Klug et al., 2008; Kern, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to EDIC Research Group, 1999; Tang and Kern, 2011; Gubitosi-Klug et al., 2008; and Kern, 2007

claim: LCLs have been shown to be a powerful model system for functional genetic studies in humans.
source: LCLs have been shown to be a powerful model system for functional genetic studies in humans (Tang and Kern, 2011; Kern, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tang and Kern, 2011 and Kern, 2007

claim: Insights into glucose-stimulated gene expression in LCLs have broad applicability to multiple tissues of interest for diabetic complications due to significant evidence supporting a shared framework for gene regulation among tissues.
source: Insights into glucose-stimulated gene expression in LCLs have broad applicability to multiple tissues of interest for diabetic complications (even in the retina as we have shown) due to significant evidence supporting a shared framework for gene regulation among tissues (GTEx Consortium, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to GTEx Consortium, 2015

claim: Altering the levels of FLCN expression impacts risk of diabetic retinopathy.
source: We show that altering the levels of FLCN expression impacts risk of diabetic retinopathy.
evidence: Supported by Mendelian randomization analysis

claim: Aggregating independent eQTLs for the same gene revealed an enriched association that may otherwise have been missed by a conventional GWAS approach.
source: Aggregating independent eQTLs for the same gene (that are not in high linkage disequilibrium) revealed an enriched association that may otherwise have been missed by a conventional GWAS approach (Wu et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2018b

claim: The Multiple Tissue Human Expression Resource (MuTHER) LCL study revealed a large impact of common environmental exposure, stemming from shared sample handling, on gene expression in twin LCLs.
source: The Multiple Tissue Human Expression Resource (MuTHER) LCL study revealed a large impact of common environmental exposure, stemming from shared sample handling, on gene expression in twin LCLs (Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wright et al., 2014

claim: Heterogeneous genomic alterations have been identified in lymphoblastoid cells that increase with passaging.
source: Moreover, as a cell line, heterogeneous genomic alterations have been identified in lymphoblastoid cells that increase with passaging, thereby raising the concern that this can lead to variability in their transcriptome (Ben-David et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ben-David et al., 2018

claim: Genomic changes have only a minor effect on genotypic frequencies with a 99.63% genotype concordance between lymphoblastoid cells and their parent leukocytes.
source: Additionally, genomic changes have only a minor effect on genotypic frequencies with a 99.63% genotype concordance between lymphoblastoid cells and their parent leukocytes.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge

claim: Mendelian error rates in levels of heterozygosity are not significantly different between LCLs and their primary B-lymphocyte cells of origin.
source: Mendelian error rates in levels of heterozygosity are not significantly different between LCLs and their primary B-lymphocyte cells of origin (McCarthy et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCarthy et al., 2016

claim: For complex trait associations in general and for those specifically in the retina, eQTL that are shared between tissues explain a greater proportion of associations than tissue-specific eQTL.
source: For complex trait associations in general and for those specifically in the retina, eQTL that are shared between tissues explain a greater proportion of associations than tissue-specific eQTL (Gamazon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamazon et al., 2018

claim: Shared tissue eQTL are enriched among genetic associations with age-related macular degeneration.
source: For instance, shared tissue eQTL are enriched among genetic associations with age-related macular degeneration, another common retinal disease, despite the high tissue specificity of the disease (Ratnapriya et al., 2019; Unlu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ratnapriya et al., 2019 and Unlu et al., 2019

claim: FLCN is expressed in the ganglion cell layer, neuronal cells of the inner nuclear layer, and faintly in the outer nuclear layer of the retina.
source: FLCN (green) is evident in the ganglion cell layer (GCL), neuronal cells of the inner nuclear layer (INL), and faintly in the outer nuclear layer (ONL).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: FLCN colocalizes with CD31, a marker of endothelial cells, confirming FLCN expression in retinal blood vessels.
source: Colocalization of FLCN with CD31 (red), a marker of endothelial cells, confirms FLCN expression in retinal blood vessels (white arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: All study individuals had type 1 diabetes and were Caucasian, and 60% were female.
source: All individuals had T1D and were Caucasian, and 60% were female.
evidence: Supported by participant demographics

claim: The power to detect a 2 fold change difference in gene expression between the two retinopathy groups with a paired analysis given the sample size and using a type I error rate of 0.05 is 95%.
source: The power to detect a 2 FC difference in gene expression between the two retinopathy groups (retinopathy vs. no retinopathy) (RGpdr–ndr) with a paired analysis given our sample size and using a type I error rate of 0.05 is 95% (as supported by our prior work Grassi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by power calculation and citation to Grassi et al., 2016
